sections.heading: M1: Foundations and system components
sections.summary: Modeling and simulation is a problem-based discipline supporting repeated hypothesis testing; its four precepts are modeling, simulation, visualization, and analysis. A system is a collection of interacting or interdependent elements working toward an end, and may be physical (already existing) or notional (a proposed concept). A model represents a system; simulation imitates its behavior over time. The overall M&S process develops a model, executes it, and analyzes output to support decisions.
source_refs: M1-MAIN-Introduction to Modeling and Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 5, 6, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14

sections.heading: M1: System structure and boundaries
sections.summary: An entity is an object of interest, an attribute is its property, and an activity causes system changes. The system state describes the entities, attributes, and activities at a point in time. Endogenous activities occur within the system boundary; exogenous activities occur outside it. The slides classify systems with exogenous activities as open, and those without them as closed. Establishing the boundary and identifying entities, attributes, and activities defines model structure; data supplies attribute values and activity relationships.
source_refs: M1-MAIN-Introduction to Modeling and Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 15, 18, 20, 22

sections.heading: M1: System behavior and modeling principles
sections.summary: Discrete state variables change at separate instants, whereas continuous state variables change continuously over time. A sampled-data system is intrinsically continuous but observed only at discrete points. Models are useful when direct study is inaccessible, dangerous, unacceptable, or impossible because the system does not yet exist. Block building divides a system into interconnected parts; relevance selects important aspects, accuracy demands correct information, and aggregation combines individual entities into larger ones.
source_refs: M1-MAIN-Introduction to Modeling and Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 9, 20, 21, 25

sections.heading: M1: Analytical solutions and simulation
sections.summary: Simple models can sometimes be evaluated analytically using mathematics; numerical simulation can evaluate complex models and gather data to estimate their properties. Simulation facilitates testing alternatives, diagnosing interactions, and identifying bottlenecks without changing the real system. Limitations include the expertise, time, and cost needed to build and interpret models. Simulation is not inherently inexpensive or fast, despite the broad comparison on page 33.
source_refs: M1-MAIN-Introduction to Modeling and Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 26, 32, 33, 34, 35

sections.heading: M1: Worked falling-object model and slide correction
sections.summary: With initial height s=1000 ft, initial upward velocity v=100 ft/s, and acceleration -32 ft/s², h(t)=-16t²+100t+1000 and velocity is 100-32t. At t=1 s, h=1084 ft; at t=2 s, h=1136 ft. Page 13's table instead shows 1052 and 972: these do not match the displayed code. The code comment also swaps the meanings of v and s; v is initial velocity and s is initial height.
source_refs: M1-MAIN-Introduction to Modeling and Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 11, 13

sections.heading: M1: Model classifications and the development cycle
sections.summary: Models can be static or dynamic, deterministic or stochastic, and continuous or discrete. A deterministic simulation produces a unique output for a specified input; a stochastic simulation uses random inputs and requires statistical analysis of random outputs. The model-code-execute-analyze cycle associates modeling, development, computational, and data/information technologies with the respective phases. Probability and statistics provide random variates for uncertain inputs and methods for analyzing stochastic output.
source_refs: M1-MAIN-Introduction to Modeling and Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 30, 38, 39, 57

sections.heading: M1: Simulation approaches
sections.summary: Monte Carlo simulation repeatedly samples input distributions and computes outputs to examine output variability. Continuous simulation represents variables as continuous functions of time and often uses differential equations. Discrete-event simulation changes system variables at distinct event times and advances from one event to the next. These methods differ in their treatment of inputs and time; randomness is not required of every simulation.
source_refs: M1-MAIN-Introduction to Modeling and Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 42, 43, 44, 57

sections.heading: M1: Fidelity, resolution, and modeling paradigms
sections.summary: Fidelity describes how closely a model matches reality; low fidelity can be acceptable for aspects unimportant to the study. Resolution or granularity is the level of detail. Physics-based models derive equations from physical principles; finite element modeling decomposes complex objects into smaller elements. Data-based models use data describing the subject; agent-based modeling investigates interacting entities and social phenomena; aggregate modeling combines smaller objects or actions; hybrid modeling combines paradigms.
source_refs: M1-MAIN-Introduction to Modeling and Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 45, 46, 48, 49, 50

sections.heading: M1: Simulation participation and applications
sections.summary: Live simulation involves real people operating real systems; virtual simulation involves real people operating simulated systems; constructive simulation uses real inputs that simulated people execute in simulated systems. Training aims at learning, analysis examines system behavior and performance, and experimentation explores solution spaces. Engineering supports design and testing, while acquisition evaluates proposed systems and cost-effectiveness across the system life cycle.
source_refs: M1-MAIN-Introduction to Modeling and Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 51, 52, 53, 55, 56

sections.heading: M1: MATLAB basics
sections.summary: MATLAB stands for Matrix Laboratory and supports mathematical computation, visualization, and programming. The workspace displays variables and command history records entered commands. Variable names begin with a letter, may contain letters, digits, and underscores, and are case-sensitive; avoid naming variables after built-in functions. help documents functions, who lists variables, whos provides more details, and clear removes variables. Numeric values default to double; logical values represent true or false.
source_refs: M1-MAIN-Introduction to Modeling and Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 73, 80, 81, 82, 83, 84

sections.heading: M1: MATLAB arrays and indexing
sections.summary: An r-by-c matrix has r rows and c columns; a row vector has one row and a column vector has one column. MATLAB indexing starts at 1, and matrix subscripts specify row before column. size returns dimensions, numel counts all elements, and length returns the largest dimension for a matrix. reshape changes dimensions; fliplr reverses columns, flipud reverses rows, rot90 rotates counterclockwise, and repmat tiles copies.
source_refs: M1-MAIN-Introduction to Modeling and Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 93, 95, 97, 98, 99, 100, 101, 102, 103, 104

sections.heading: M1: MATLAB calculations and source cautions
sections.summary: For a matrix, sum, prod, min, and max operate down columns by default; specifying dimension 2 operates rowwise. Array multiplication, division, and exponentiation use dotted operators such as .*; matrix multiplication uses * and requires the left column count to equal the right row count. The result has the left matrix’s row count and the right matrix’s column count. Page 88 incorrectly implies sign(0) is -1: it is 0. Page 113 states arrays must be the same size, but compatible sizes can also be implicitly expanded in modern MATLAB. Page 107 overgeneralizes elementwise function behavior: reduction functions such as sum do not preserve the input size.
source_refs: M1-MAIN-Introduction to Modeling and Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 88, 107, 109, 111, 113, 114, 116, 117

sections.heading: M2: Sets and functions
sections.summary:
A set contains distinct elements; a subset contains only elements of its reference set, and disjoint sets share no elements. Union includes either set, intersection includes both, A−B includes elements only in A, and A’s complement contains the elements of the universal set outside A.

Worked example: U={2,4,6,8,10,12}, A={2,4,10}, B={4,6,8,10}. A∪B={2,4,6,8,10}; A∩B={4,10}; A−B={2}; B−A={6,8}; Aᶜ={6,8,12}.

A function maps each domain element to exactly one codomain element. Its range is the set actually reached; onto means the range equals the codomain, and one-to-one means distinct inputs have distinct outputs. A function has an inverse on its full codomain when it is both one-to-one and onto. For f(x)=mx+b on the reals with m≠0, f⁻¹(y)=(y−b)/m.
source_refs: M2-MAIN-Discrete Event Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12

sections.heading: M2: Probability and random variables
sections.summary:
A probability space consists of sample space S, an event σ-algebra, and probability measure P. Events are measurable subsets of S; P(S)=1, and probabilities of disjoint events add. A σ-algebra includes S and is closed under complements and countable unions. Page 15’s claim that any σ-algebra on k outcomes has 2^k events is too broad: this count applies to the full power set.

For the three-sided die, P(B)=1/6, P(C)=1/3 and P(D)=1/2; therefore P(B or C)=1/2 and P(C or D)=5/6. The full event collection has 2³=8 events.

A random variable assigns real numbers to outcomes. Its cumulative distribution F(x)=P(X≤x) is nondecreasing, and P(a<X≤b)=F(b)−F(a). For a continuous distribution with density f, interval probabilities are areas under f, and F(x) is the integral of f up to x.
source_refs: M2-MAIN-Discrete Event Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 22

sections.heading: M2: Distributions and random variates
sections.summary:
Uniform(a,b) has constant density over its interval; triangular(a,m,b) is useful when minimum, most likely value, and maximum are known but the exact shape is not. Exponential interarrival times have mean m and rate λ=1/m; for x≥0, P(X>x)=exp(−λx). Normal(m,σ) describes variability around a mean, with σ the standard deviation.

Page 25’s displayed exponential density omits the rate multiplier: the normalized density is λ exp(−λx) for x≥0. A continuous uniform distribution gives equal probabilities to equal-length intervals, not a positive equal probability to each individual real value.

Simulation first generates a uniform random number and transforms it into a random variate with the desired distribution. A linear congruential generator uses Zₖ₊₁=(aZₖ+c) mod m and Uₖ=Zₖ/m; its integers repeat after a period no longer than m, so parameter and seed selection matter.
source_refs: M2-MAIN-Discrete Event Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30

sections.heading: M2: Input and output modeling
sections.summary:
Structural modeling identifies entities, locations, resources and processes; data modeling supplies quantitative inputs such as interarrival times, service times, schedules, failures and travel times.

Direct sample use preserves recorded values but limited samples may miss rare possibilities and repeated retrieval can be costly. An empirical distribution represents observed samples and can generate arbitrarily long streams, but cannot produce unobserved outliers. A fitted theoretical distribution can smooth sample irregularities, but fitting takes effort and a good fit may not exist.

Output data analysis converts simulation output into information about system performance; the slides introduce the confidence interval for a mean and identify more complex analysis situations without giving a detailed procedure.
source_refs: M2-MAIN-Discrete Event Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37, 39

sections.heading: M2: DES elements and clock advance
sections.summary:
Discrete-event simulation represents a system whose modeled state changes at separated event times. The module describes its DES examples as stochastic and dynamic; stochasticity is not inherent to every possible DES model. An entity moves through the system, attributes carry entity-specific information, resources provide service, and queues hold entities waiting for occupied resources. An event changes system state.

Resource capacity is the number served simultaneously; utilization is busy time divided by total observed time. The simulation executive controls clock advance and event execution. A next-event list holds scheduled event times; timing selects the next event, the event routine updates state, accumulators gather performance information, and the report generator summarizes results.

Fixed-increment advancement updates at chosen time steps and can force between-step events onto a boundary. Next-event advancement moves directly to the earliest scheduled event, updates state there, and skips inactive intervals. The simulation clock represents elapsed simulated time, not necessarily elapsed wall-clock time.
source_refs: M2-MAIN-Discrete Event Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 44, 48, 50, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56, 57, 58, 60, 61, 62

sections.heading: M2: Queue behavior and worked example
sections.summary:
A queueing model describes arrivals, service and the rule for selecting waiting customers. Variation in arrival and service times can cause waiting. FCFS/FIFO serves the earliest arrival first; LIFO/LCFS serves the most recent first; priority and shortest-processing-time rules select differently. Page 66 mistakenly labels last-in-first-out as FIFO; it should be LIFO.

Balking means deciding not to enter a line, reneging means leaving after joining but before service, and jockeying means switching lines. A design may balance the cost of service capacity against the cost of waiting. Systems may have single or multiple servers and single or multiple service phases.

For the page 78–79 single-server FCFS example, arrivals are 0,4,5,9,11,15 and service times are 2,3,1,4,2,3. Service starts at 0,4,7,9,13,15 and ends at 2,7,8,13,15,18. Waits are 0,0,2,0,2,0; total wait is 4 and mean wait is 4/6. Customer 5 spends 15−11=4 time units in the system.

For an initially idle single server, startᵢ=max(arrivalᵢ, endᵢ₋₁), waitᵢ=startᵢ−arrivalᵢ, endᵢ=startᵢ+serviceᵢ, and time in system=endᵢ−arrivalᵢ. Idle time before a customer is max(0, arrivalᵢ−endᵢ₋₁). Page 77 reverses the waiting-time subtraction and incorrectly says the first service always begins at zero; it begins at the first arrival when the initially idle server is available. Its interarrival indexing is also inconsistent.
source_refs: M2-MAIN-Discrete Event Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 63, 64, 65, 66, 68, 69, 70, 71, 72, 73, 74, 75, 77, 78, 79

sections.heading: M3: Continuous systems and modeling strategy
sections.summary:
A continuous-state model describes variables evolving over continuous time; its input and output need not be identical or constant. Page 5 incorrectly claims signals are the same and do not vary. Applications listed include dam and tunnel engineering, missile trajectories, airport passenger flow, and business planning.

Translate the system into quantitative equations, then choose a numerical implementation. State variables must collectively capture the relevant dynamics to the accuracy required; state equations describe their change, often with time as the independent variable. Output equations specify quantities requested by users.
source_refs: M3-MAIN - Modeling Continuous Systems.pdf, PDF p. 5, 7, 9, 10, 11

sections.heading: M3: Reservoir and differential-equation classes
sections.summary:
For the slide’s ideal infinite-capacity reservoir, q is the contents, x is signed input rate, dq/dt = x(t), and y = q. Thus q(t) = q(0) + integral from 0 to t of x(s) ds; if q(0)=4 and x=2 for three time units, q(3)=10.

The slides classify predator–prey models as first-order ODEs, orbital motion and RLC circuits as second-order ODEs, and wave or heat models as PDEs. A second-order ODE can be expressed as a first-order system by introducing velocity as another state.
source_refs: M3-MAIN - Modeling Continuous Systems.pdf, PDF p. 6, 8, 10, 11

sections.heading: M3: Orbit states and outputs
sections.summary: For a planetary orbit the state vector contains three-dimensional position and velocity. Position derivatives are velocities; under the slide’s central-gravity model acceleration is −GM r-vector/|r-vector|³. The state can be used to calculate desired outputs such as distance or speed.
source_refs: M3-MAIN - Modeling Continuous Systems.pdf, PDF p. 9, 11

sections.heading: M3: Predator–prey dynamics
sections.summary:
With prey x and predators y, the general model is dx/dt = x f(x,y), dy/dt = y g(x,y). For positive populations, f and g are per-capita growth rates. Increasing predators suppresses prey growth; increasing prey supports predator growth. The qualitative cycle goes from abundant prey to more predators, falling prey, predator starvation, and prey recovery.

The Lotka–Volterra choice is f=b−py and g=rx−d, giving dx/dt=x(b−py) and dy/dt=y(rx−d). With positive parameters the positive equilibrium is (x,y)=(d/r,b/p). For b=p=r=d=1 it is (1,1), matching the slide’s phase-plane example.

For positive x,y the conserved quantity is C=b ln(y)−py−rx+d ln(x). Page 16 omits r before x; its expression is valid when r=1, as on page 17. The correction follows by differentiating C using the two state equations. Parameter values and initial conditions determine the trajectory.
source_refs: M3-MAIN - Modeling Continuous Systems.pdf, PDF p. 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17

sections.heading: M3: Numerical integration
sections.summary:
Forward Euler approximates the derivative using the current slope: x(n+1)=x(n)+h f(t(n),x(n)). For x′=x, x(0)=1 and h=0.2, one Euler step gives 1.2.

The slide’s Runge–Kutta formula is the explicit midpoint RK2 method: t_mid=t0+h/2, x_mid=x0+(h/2)f(t0,x0), then x1=x0+h f(t_mid,x_mid). For the same example, x_mid=1.1 and x1=1.22. These are approximations, not exact solutions.
source_refs: M3-MAIN - Modeling Continuous Systems.pdf, PDF p. 18, 19

sections.heading: M3: MATLAB scripts, functions, input and output
sections.summary:
Scripts and function files both use the .m extension. Scripts execute commands in the workspace; functions can take inputs, return outputs, and use local internal variables. The editor can be opened with edit or edit followed by a filename.

input("Enter a number") reads a numerical expression; input("Enter text", "s") reads text. disp(X) displays a value without the variable name, whereas fprintf supports formatted output such as %s for text and %d for an integer; \n produces a newline.
source_refs: M3-MAIN - Modeling Continuous Systems.pdf, PDF p. 27, 29, 30, 34, 35, 36, 38, 40

sections.heading: M3: MATLAB arrays and plots
sections.summary:
Examples include row vectors a=1:2, column vectors b=(1:3)' and matrix addition A+B. The example with a and b uses compatible implicit expansion to form a 3-by-2 result.

To graph a function, define x and y, then use plot(x,y). xlabel, ylabel, title, and grid on annotate the figure; axis equal uses equal scales and axis square makes the plot box square. A LineSpec can specify color, line style, and marker.
source_refs: M3-MAIN - Modeling Continuous Systems.pdf, PDF p. 33, 47, 48

sections.heading: M3: MATLAB selection and loops
sections.summary:
if, elseif, else and end select branches; switch selects cases and otherwise handles unmatched cases. The age example on page 62 does not classify ages 20 and 60 correctly and can classify nonpositive ages as senior; check boundaries explicitly rather than copying it.

The page 61 parity example is erroneous: % starts a MATLAB comment, not a remainder operation, and both branches print Even number. Use mod(x,2)==0 for even integers and print Odd number in the other branch.

menu displays choices and returns the selected button number. A for loop iterates over a supplied sequence such as 1:10 or 1.0:-0.2:0.0; a while loop repeats while its condition is true.
source_refs: M3-MAIN - Modeling Continuous Systems.pdf, PDF p. 60, 61, 62, 63, 64, 65, 66, 67

sections.heading: M4: Monte Carlo fundamentals
sections.summary:
Monte Carlo simulation uses repeated random sampling of input variables and model evaluations to estimate an output distribution or numerical quantity. It arose in the 1940s at Los Alamos in atomic physics and is used in risk analysis and decision-making across engineering, finance, and other fields.

Random inputs make Monte Carlo useful for uncertainty, but it is not universally superior to deterministic methods. The slide's assertion that the result must already be known is misleading: the model and sampling assumptions must be specified, while the quantity of interest is generally estimated. The slide's historical name 'Ulman' refers to Stanislaw Ulam.
source_refs: M4-MAIN - Monte Carlo Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 6, 7, 9, 10

sections.heading: M4: Model types, applications, and precision
sections.summary:
The module illustrates simple Monte Carlo, mixture modelling, two-stage Monte Carlo, and Markov chains. Its two-stage diagram has an initial set of nodes, with one node feeding a further stage; a Markov chain depicts transitions among states.

Applications illustrated include numerical integration, distribution properties and tail probabilities, optimization, and physical simulation. A fixed grid with N points per dimension requires N^D points in D dimensions; random sampling is an alternative. Randomized optimization can escape local minima, without guaranteeing a global optimum.

Monte Carlo estimates are approximate. For ordinary independent sampling with finite variance, standard error typically scales as 1/sqrt(N): four times as many runs halve the standard error. Greater precision can therefore be computationally expensive.
source_refs: M4-MAIN - Monte Carlo Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15

sections.heading: M4: Four-step procedure and ingredients
sections.summary:
Define the input distributions; randomly generate input sets; apply the deterministic model to each set; aggregate the resulting outputs. The slide's required ingredients are probability distributions, a random-number generator, a sampling rule, a scoring rule, and an estimate of statistical error.

For example, to estimate P(X > α), draw X from its specified distribution and average the indicator 1[X > α]. This estimates the tail integral ∫α∞ f(x) dx; it need not be known before the experiment.
source_refs: M4-MAIN - Monte Carlo Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 12, 17, 18

sections.heading: M4: Estimating π with a quarter circle
sections.summary:
Sample points uniformly in the unit square 0 ≤ x,y ≤ 1. A point is inside the quarter unit circle when x² + y² ≤ 1. Its area is π/4, so the proportion of points inside approximates π/4 and π̂ = 4H/N, where H is the hit count and N is the total number of points.

Worked example: 785 hits among 1,000 points give π̂ = 4(785/1000) = 3.14. This is an illustrative sample estimate, not an exact value. The diagram concerns a quarter circle, although the slide labels its numerator as points inside the 'circle'.
source_refs: M4-MAIN - Monte Carlo Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 19, 20, 21

sections.heading: M4: Sensitivity analysis
sections.summary:
Sensitivity analysis studies how output uncertainty is associated with sources of input uncertainty and identifies influential inputs. It can reveal model errors and important input bounds, prioritize research, and support model simplification.

Derivative-based sensitivity is computationally efficient but local to the point of evaluation. For nonlinear models, sensitivity may change across the input range; a local derivative alone need not represent global behavior, although it can still be useful locally.
source_refs: M4-MAIN - Monte Carlo Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 22, 23

sections.heading: M4: MATLAB file input and output
sections.summary:
The slides list delimited ASCII, diary logs, formatted output using fprintf, MEX-based file access, and spreadsheet export. For a numeric matrix A, save data.dat A -ascii writes ASCII numeric data; dlmwrite('data.out', A, ' ') writes a space-delimited array. These are the slide's legacy commands.

A normal save overwrites the target; the example save testfile.dat mat2 -ascii -append appends data. Saving a character array with -ascii writes numeric character codes rather than the original text. In the displayed numeric ASCII example, load testfile.dat creates testfile; rows must have consistent numbers of values.

In the time-temperature example, load timetemp.dat creates the array, time = timetemp(1,:) selects its first row, temp = timetemp(2,:) selects its second, and plot(time,temp,'k*') plots black asterisks.
source_refs: M4-MAIN - Monte Carlo Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38

sections.heading: M4: MATLAB 2D and 3D plots
sections.summary:
For a function, define x, compute y = f(x), then plot(x,y). xlabel, ylabel, and title annotate the plot; grid on displays a grid. axis equal gives equal scale factors, while axis square makes the plotting box square; these are different settings.

A LineSpec can combine color, line style, and marker. For example plot(x,y,'r*') marks points with red asterisks, and hold on allows a subsequent plot to be overlaid. The module also shows bar(x,y), and plot(x,y,x,g,'.-') with a legend for sine and cosine.

For 3D data, plot3(x,y,z) plots coordinate vectors and zlabel labels the third axis. The slide also lists bar3 and stem3, and recommends grid and 3D rotation to aid viewing.
source_refs: M4-MAIN - Monte Carlo Simulation.pdf, PDF p. 43, 44, 45, 46, 48, 49, 50, 51

sections.heading: M5: Model types and examples
sections.summary:
Fishwick’s categories include declarative models focused on states and events; functional models connect components directionally through mathematical relationships; constraint models emphasize relationships and physical balances rather than direction; spatial models represent spaces or entities within spaces. Page 5 repeats the functional definition under declarative models; use the state-event description and page 6 examples instead.

The Easy Pass deceleration functional diagram uses a = dv/dt and v = dx/dt: an acceleration signal is integrated to velocity (initial condition v₀), then velocity to position. The constraint example adds ½mv² = F_f d; for constant friction magnitude and stopping from initial speed v, d = mv²/(2F_f). For example, m = 1000 kg, v = 10 m/s, F_f = 5000 N gives d = 10 m. This assumes friction accounts for the kinetic energy lost.
source_refs: M5-MAIN - Systems Modeling.pdf, PDF p. 5, 6, 7, 8

sections.heading: M5: Conceptual and hybrid models
sections.summary:
A conceptual model communicates the target system’s main functionality and distinctive qualities quickly, often informally in a picture or one or two paragraphs. The Easy Pass example uses both textual and graphical representations.

A multimodel or hybrid connects several models, potentially of different types, in a network. Different abstractions support different questions or different phases of a complex system. In a concept map, nodes represent concepts or elements, directed arrows indicate interactions, and arrow labels describe their nature.
source_refs: M5-MAIN - Systems Modeling.pdf, PDF p. 10, 11, 12, 13

sections.heading: M5: Formal and semiformal tools
sections.summary:
A formalism specifies precise rules for modeling and simulation; its formal models support unambiguous mathematical analysis, often automated, but can be complex and tedious to design and implement. Semiformal representations trade some precision for ease of use while retaining some analytical capability. The slide’s phrase ‘less unambiguity’ is confusing; the intended contrast is less precision than formal models.

UML is a standardized, semiformal, object-oriented graphic notation for system and software structure and behavior. The slide lists use cases, activity diagrams, class diagrams, sequence diagrams, and statecharts.
source_refs: M5-MAIN - Systems Modeling.pdf, PDF p. 14, 15

sections.heading: M5: Verification and validation
sections.summary:
Verification checks whether conceptual-model requirements were correctly translated into the executable model and whether it runs reliably. Techniques include automated debugging, peer code review, and stress tests at minimum and maximum boundary conditions; debugging may struggle with semantic errors.

Validation asks whether the model approximates its target system sufficiently well to provide useful results. Compare model and target outputs statistically when possible; when the target does not exist, use a similar system or expert judgment. Expert judgment of outputs is face validation.
source_refs: M5-MAIN - Systems Modeling.pdf, PDF p. 16, 17

sections.heading: M5: Operations research
sections.summary:
Operations research applies mathematical models to complex systems to optimize performance and support decisions, such as maximizing profit or minimizing cost. Formulate the problem, develop a mathematical model, then solve it to search for an optimum.

Linear programming is a deterministic method using a linear objective and linear constraints. Stochastic operations-research methods include Markov chains and queuing theory.
source_refs: M5-MAIN - Systems Modeling.pdf, PDF p. 18

sections.heading: M5: Simulink and worked block examples
sections.summary:
Simulink integrates with MATLAB and provides a graphical editor, customizable block libraries, and solvers for modeling and simulating dynamic systems. MATLAB algorithms can be included in models and results exported to MATLAB. Applications include pre-hardware exploration, reusable components, hardware-in-the-loop testing, and large simulations on multicore desktops, clusters, or the cloud.

In the arithmetic block example, (1+100)+(50+100)−75−10 = 166 and 166×(10×1) = 1660. A greater-than comparison with 5000 returns 0 (false). In the other example, √16 + 3² + sign(−5) = 4+9−1 = 12, so equality to 12 returns 1 (true).

Page 30 is labeled arithmetic but shows string concatenation and length, while its comparison explanation is unrelated. The visible text ‘Hello FEU Tech’ contains 14 characters including spaces; the displayed length 16 is not explained by the visible text, so hidden spaces or different inputs cannot be established from the slide.
source_refs: M5-MAIN - Systems Modeling.pdf, PDF p. 25, 29, 30, 31

sections.heading: M6: Visualization and graphics
sections.summary: Visualization turns information into imagery, graphs, or animation, making large or time-varying information easier to understand. In modeling and simulation it includes data analysis and visual training simulations; computer graphics is its core technology. Computer graphics generates or manipulates images using software and hardware.
source_refs: M6-MAIN-Visualization and VV and A.pdf, PDF p. 5, 6

sections.heading: M6: Graphics hardware and 3D geometry
sections.summary: Realistic graphics requires computation and memory. The slides trace dedicated workstation acceleration in the mid-1980s, 2D PC acceleration in the mid-1990s, 3D PC acceleration in the late 1990s, and programmable vertex and pixel shaders in the early 2000s. Convex polygon meshes simplify rendering: a line segment joining any two points in a convex object lies entirely within it.
source_refs: M6-MAIN-Visualization and VV and A.pdf, PDF p. 7, 23

sections.heading: M6: Coordinates and transformations
sections.summary: A point represents a location without size or shape; a vector has direction and length but no location. Graphics use Cartesian components, matrices, and homogeneous coordinates to express transformations. Affine transformations preserve collinearity and ratios of distances along a line; translation, rotation, and scaling are examples. They can represent changes in dynamic objects.
source_refs: M6-MAIN-Visualization and VV and A.pdf, PDF p. 24, 25, 26

sections.heading: M6: Synthetic cameras and projection
sections.summary: A synthetic camera maps 3D objects to a 2D projection using camera parameters. Location, target location, and up direction position and orient it; world coordinates are converted into camera coordinates. Perspective projection uses a finite center of projection and rays through object points. Parallel projection uses a direction of projection and six clipping planes; orthographic projection has a direction perpendicular to the projection plane and preserves distances and directions along that plane, useful for CAD measurements.
source_refs: M6-MAIN-Visualization and VV and A.pdf, PDF p. 38, 39, 40, 41, 42, 43, 44

sections.heading: M6: Lighting, shading, and textures
sections.summary: Rods primarily support low-light vision, while cones support color vision. Ambient light gives uniform illumination independent of location and direction. A point light radiates equally in all directions and attenuates with distance. A spotlight is specified by location, direction, and cutoff angle; a directional light models a distant source such as sunlight. Reflection describes light–object interaction, shading determines colors within polygons, and texture mapping enriches appearance without greatly increasing geometric complexity.
source_refs: M6-MAIN-Visualization and VV and A.pdf, PDF p. 46, 47, 48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53

sections.heading: M6: Graphics software
sections.summary: The slides identify OpenGL as a cross-platform low-level graphics API and Direct3D as a Microsoft 3D graphics API; they also describe OpenSceneGraph as an open-source cross-platform library, MATLAB for numerical work and visualization, and Maya for 3D modeling and animation. These slides describe historical tools and should not be treated as an up-to-date product survey. Page 57 calls Java 3D a programming language; more accurately, Java 3D is an API for 3D graphics, not the Java language itself.
source_refs: M6-MAIN-Visualization and VV and A.pdf, PDF p. 55, 56, 57, 58

sections.heading: M6: VV&A vocabulary and requirements
sections.summary: The simuland is the real object, process, or phenomenon of interest; the referent is the knowledge available about it, both quantitative and qualitative. A conceptual model documents represented and omitted aspects and assumptions, serving as a specification for an executable model. A simulation executes a model over time and produces results. Requirements, driven by intended use, specify what must be modeled and how accurately.
source_refs: M6-MAIN-Visualization and VV and A.pdf, PDF p. 62, 63, 64, 65, 66, 67, 68

sections.heading: M6: Verification, validation, and accreditation
sections.summary: Verification examines transformational accuracy: whether requirements, conceptual model, and executable implementation are consistent. Validation examines representational accuracy: how accurately the model and its results represent the simuland, including the range of credible inputs. Accreditation is a responsible authority’s official decision that a model is acceptable for a specific purpose, informed by V&V results. Neither general apparent realism nor verification alone establishes validity for every use.
source_refs: M6-MAIN-Visualization and VV and A.pdf, PDF p. 70, 71, 72

sections.heading: M6: Project types and credibility
sections.summary: A simulation study primarily seeks insight; code need not be its primary deliverable. Simulation software development delivers executable software expected to be reused and maintained. A simulation event uses existing models for a particular objective, with scenario, data, logistics, and security potentially important. Credibility concerns whether results are considered acceptable for an application and costs resources to develop; managers balance credibility requirements against available resources.
source_refs: M6-MAIN-Visualization and VV and A.pdf, PDF p. 74, 75, 76, 82

sections.heading: M6: Errors and bounds of validity
sections.summary: Type I error is not using a valid model, with likelihood called model builder’s risk. Type II is using an invalid model, with likelihood called model user’s risk. Type III is using a model valid for another purpose but inappropriate for the intended application, with likelihood called model accreditor’s risk. The gravity examples illustrate bounds of validity: a simple approximation can be adequate only over a limited range, while the gravity model depends on assumptions including negligible air resistance and proximity to Earth’s surface.
source_refs: M6-MAIN-Visualization and VV and A.pdf, PDF p. 78, 79, 80, 81

sections.heading: M6: Informal and static methods
sections.summary: Informal V&V relies on qualitative expert judgment. Inspection compares artifacts such as code against design equations; face validation compares observed results against experts’ knowledge of the simuland. The Turing test is a specialized face-validation approach for human behavior. Static methods examine characteristics without executing a simulation: data analysis checks definitions, operations, dependencies, and flows, while cause–effect graphing compares important causal relationships between simuland and conceptual model.
source_refs: M6-MAIN-Visualization and VV and A.pdf, PDF p. 83, 84, 85, 86, 87, 88, 89

sections.heading: M6: Dynamic and formal methods
sections.summary: Dynamic V&V executes models and evaluates results. Sensitivity analysis compares the magnitude and variability of outputs and can reveal influential inputs; predictive validation compares specific corresponding outcomes; comparison testing runs multiple models with the same input. Regression and hypothesis testing provide statistical approaches. Formal methods use mathematical proof: inductive assertions address executable-model correctness along execution paths, and predicate calculus can express and compare simuland and conceptual-model properties. Appropriate methods depend on the model, available data, and practical execution, and multiple methods are often combined.
source_refs: M6-MAIN-Visualization and VV and A.pdf, PDF p. 90, 91, 92, 93, 94, 95, 96, 97, 98
